endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Provide all patients, no later than the date of first service delivery, with a comprehensive Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP), including how protected health information (PHI) may be used by AI solutions, in compliance with HIPAA.

endorsements.title: Toward a responsible future: recommendations for AI-enabled clinical decision support
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
endorsements.quote: Our working group recommends creating a similar set of constructs and a parallel system for training requirements, which should be mandatory (depending on the application\u2019s envisioned end users\u2014for clinicians or laypeople) and documented and monitored as part of overall risk mitigation and legal/compliance constructs.

endorsements.title: Accelerating ambient AI scribe enterprise-scale deployment: Cleveland Clinic's novel approach to health system-industry partnership
endorsements.quote: To promote proper usage from the start and to reduce the number of clinicians who might not gain full value from the product, CCF required clinicians to receive this training before being granted access to the tool.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence in Military Graduate Medical Education: Trainee Perceptions and Current Use
evidence.outcome: Trainee AI use in daily work without prior formal AI training
evidence.effect: Only 10 of 83 respondents reported prior formal AI training; 73% disagreed their curriculum had enough. 30% used AI for diagnosis, 27% for treatment, 28% for teaching.
evidence.quote: Importantly, trainees reported utilizing AI in daily practice without training.

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether requiring AI training before granting tool access reduces harm, so support for this practice rests on two commentaries and the Cleveland Clinic ambient scribe rollout. One survey found that 10 of 83 medical trainees had formal AI training while about 30% used AI for diagnosis, which suggests untrained use is common but does not show that gating access would prevent harm.

perspectives.view: No study compares users trained before access with untrained users on errors, harm, or proper use. The one available study is a cross-sectional survey of 83 trainees at a single level of evidence. It documents the gap in training but not its consequences. The endorsements are commentaries and a framework, which count as expert opinion under GRADE.

Among 83 trainees, 30% reported using AI for diagnosis and 27% for treatment, and only 10 reported formal AI training. This shows exposure in high-stakes tasks. The survey did not measure errors or patient harm, so the size of the harm that training would prevent remains unknown.

Cleveland Clinic required clinicians to complete training before receiving ambient scribe access, and the commentary describes this as a way to promote proper use from the start. The report does not give completion rates, delays to access, or later usage quality. It therefore shows that an access gate can be run at enterprise scale, not that it changes behavior.

The CHAI framework passage cited for this recommendation concerns giving patients a Notice of Privacy Practices under HIPAA. It does not address clinician training or access controls. Direct endorsement for training as an access condition comes from the two commentaries, one of which recommends that training be mandatory, documented, and monitored as part of risk mitigation.

The Cleveland Clinic account suggests that tying access to training completion is feasible within a large deployment. No source reports staff time, training cost, or effects on adoption speed. Leaders would need to budget for building training by tool and user role and for tracking completion, as the working group commentary proposes.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare users who completed pre-access training with users who did not, measuring misuse, documentation errors, safety events, and time to productive use. These studies should also report the burden of training and how completion is tracked across different tools and user roles.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The hazard survey covered graduate medical education trainees and did not report on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so the evidence cannot say whether training requirements affect care quality for these groups.
